name: Self-Serving Bias
description: People tend to credit successes to their own ability or character while blaming failures on situation, luck, or unfair circumstances. The same outcome data gets narrated differently depending on whether it protects the self.
design_relevance_note: Relevant when interpreting user research, creator analytics, employee retros, and customer narratives: people may explain wins and losses in ego-protective ways that distort what actually caused behavior.
prevalence_note: A standard named bias in psychology education and workplace retrospectives, and often invoked when interpreting post-hoc stories about why products, campaigns, or people succeeded or failed.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of 266 studies (503 independent effect sizes) found a large self-serving attributional bias overall: people made more internal, stable, and global attributions for positive events than for negative ones. The bias was pervasive but moderated by age, culture, and psychopathology.
findings.effect_size: Average d = 0.96 overall; Asian samples d = 0.30 vs. U.S. d = 1.05 and Western d = 0.70
findings.source_title: Is There a Universal Positivity Bias in Attributions? A Meta-Analytic Review of Individual, Developmental, and Cultural Differences in the Self-Serving Attributional Bias.

applications.title: Kriss, Loewenstein, Wang & Weber's climate-negotiation fairness study
applications.description: Surveying college students in the United States and China, researchers found each group displayed a nationalistic self-serving bias when judging a fair distribution of the economic burden of reducing greenhouse-gas emissions -- each nation's students judged outcomes favoring their own country as more 'fair.' When the researchers disguised the problem and the identity of the parties involved, participants' fairness judgments stopped being influenced by national interest, showing the bias was specifically about self-interest, not a genuine disagreement about what fairness means.
applications.industry_context: public policy / international climate negotiation (not a digital-product context)
applications.ethical_note: A policy-perception research finding with no persuasion or product-design dimension -- included because it's an unusually clean, real, peer-reviewed demonstration of the bias's real-world stakes (international climate policy) rather than the more commonly available student/lab demonstrations of the effect.
